I would code Ryan’s absence **UA**, while urgently asking an appropriate payroll or management contact to review the consequence before 12:00.

Ryan was not ill, so SC is incorrect. His sister is not a dependant under the definitions provided: she is not in one of the listed relationship categories and does not live with him. BRV does not apply, and the absence was not booked in advance. That leaves UA under the stated rules, even though Ryan had a compelling reason to be absent and called his team leader.

I would immediately email payroll and an available manager, explain that this coding will trigger a termination letter, and ask whether an authorised person can pause the letter or review Ryan’s circumstances. I would not assume the team leader will see an email before payroll runs, or that sending one stops the process.

I would also add a factual note that Ryan called at 05:40 and was assisting his sister during an unexpected early labour. The note does not change the code or the automatic outcome, but preserves information relevant to a review.

If nobody responds in time, I would still correct the code to UA. Leaving it as SC would knowingly submit an inaccurate sickness record; I have no stated authority to waive the probation rule. I would be clear that, without an intervention, the payroll run is expected to produce and send the termination letter.
